**The Weight of Words**

Words are like stones—some smooth and round, worn by time and the hands of strangers; others jagged, sharp enough to draw blood if you’re not careful. I’ve always believed that language is both a bridge and a barrier. It connects us, but it also separates. A single word can lift a heart to the heavens or crush it beneath the weight of misunderstanding.

I remember the first time I realized how fragile words could be. I was twelve, sitting in a dimly lit library, surrounded by books that smelled of old paper and quiet wisdom. I had just read a poem about a dying tree, and for some reason, the image of it—its branches clawing at the sky, its roots tangled in the earth—stayed with me. I tried to write my own poem about it, but every attempt felt like a lie. The words were there, but they didn’t *mean* anything. Not really.

That’s the thing about words—they’re not just symbols on a page. They carry the weight of every emotion, every memory, every half-formed thought that flickers through the mind. A word like *love* can mean everything to one person and nothing to another. A word like *home* can be a place, a feeling, or a wound that never quite heals.

I’ve spent years collecting words like someone might collect seashells—each one unique, each one holding the echo of the ocean. Some are bright and colorful, others dull and cracked. Some fit perfectly in my palm; others cut me when I’m not looking. But I keep them all, because you never know when a word will save you.

There was a time when I thought silence was the opposite of words. But silence is just another kind of language—a language of absence, of what isn’t said. Sometimes, the most powerful thing you can do is not speak at all. To let the weight of the unsaid hang in the air between you and another person. To let them fill it with their own words, their own meanings.

I’ve learned that words can be weapons, too. A carefully chosen insult can linger for years. A lie told with a smile can unravel lives. But words can also heal. A kind word at the right moment can be the difference between despair and hope. A story shared can make someone feel less alone.

I wonder sometimes if words are alive. Not in the way that trees or animals are alive, but in the way that fire is alive—something that spreads, that consumes, that can warm a room or burn a house to the ground. Words have a life of their own. They grow, they change, they take on new meanings with every person who hears them.

I’ve written and rewritten the same sentence a hundred times, trying to get it just right. Trying to make it mean exactly what I want it to mean. But language is slippery. It resists. It bends. It means something different to everyone who reads it.

Maybe that’s the beauty of it. Words are never just one thing. They’re a conversation between the writer and the reader, between the past and the future, between the self and the world. They’re never finished. They’re always growing, always changing.

I could write for a thousand more words and still not say everything I want to say. But maybe that’s the point. Maybe the real magic isn’t in the words themselves, but in the space between them. In the silence. In the unsaid.

So here I am, writing these words, knowing they’ll never be enough. But that’s okay. Because words are never enough. They’re just the best we have.
